extracted.intended_audience: legislators, political philosophers, and students of political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for founding, organising, and educating an ideal city-state (polis): necessary institutions, distribution of roles and property, urban siting and fortification, public rituals and meals, and laws on marriage and education aimed at producing virtuous citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential parts/functions of a state
rubrics_metrics.description: A city requires certain absolutely necessary things: a population, a portion of territory, a constitution, a power to command obedience and defend from external attack, a revenue for internal needs and war, a religious establishment, and courts to determine criminal and civil causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are 'absolutely necessary' for a city to secure independence and self-protection; without any of them the ends of the state cannot be obtained. Each is briefly characterized (e.g., revenue for war and internal necessities; courts as chief concern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of employments/occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether employments (husbandmen, artificers, soldiers, senators, judges, priests) are common to all or appropriated to particular persons; in the best state certain employments (mechanic trades, merchandise, husbandry) should not be performed by citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best-governed states require citizens free from ignoble employments so they may pursue virtue; soldiers, senators, and judges may be the same or different persons depending on required abilities (courage vs judgment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who should be citizens (property and status)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizens proper are those engaged in noble, honourable, and virtuous employments; no mechanic or those in ignoble trades ought to be admitted to the rights of a citizen; landed property should belong to those who partake in government (soldiers, council).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because happiness requires virtue, and virtue is undermined by ignoble occupations, the legislator should reserve political rights and land for those fit for citizenship; husbandmen and artisans serve as labourers (possibly slaves or servants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Priesthood as a distinct class
rubrics_metrics.description: Priests compose a rank by themselves and should not be counted among husbandmen or mechanics; reverence to the gods is becoming of every state; those employed in sacred service should have nothing else to do and be of age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign priestly business to elders; provide separate public tables/buildings for priests near temples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of husbandmen from soldiers and property division
rubrics_metrics.description: Husbandmen (farmers) should be a separate order from soldiers; land should be divided into public and private halves, with further subdivision so each citizen has land both near the city and at the extremity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Half of the public land should support worship of the gods, the other half common meals; subdivision equalizes interests and induces concerted defence—avoids border inhabitants neglecting or overvaluing border wars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of slaves and servants for agriculture
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer slaves (not of the same nation) or barbarian servants for husbandry; slaves for private property belong to the individual, those cultivating public territory belong to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Barbarian or foreign slaves are preferred as they will be more laborious and less prone to novelty; promise of liberty as reward for services is appropriate and to be discussed later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common meals/public tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Common meals are proper in well-regulated cities; all citizens ought to partake of them; the expense of religious worship and common meals should be defrayed by the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common meals foster civic unity but poor citizens may not be able to furnish their share from personal resources, hence public support/appropriation is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: City siting: health, season, defence, and water
rubrics_metrics.description: Position the city to consult health (east-facing best, north second), preparedness for government/business and defence in war, and proximity to water (rivers or large cisterns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Air and water chiefly influence health; waters should be apportioned to different purposes and drinking water kept separate from other uses. Good position influences both health and defensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortification strategy depends on regime
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper fortifications differ by constitution: a lofty citadel suits monarchy/oligarchy, a plain-built city suits a democracy, many strong places suit an aristocracy; walls are generally prudent and should be both defence and ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claiming walls unnecessary is mistaken; modern defensive improvements and philosophical invention should be applied to fortifications; being well prepared deters attack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private house forms and mixed urban design
rubrics_metrics.description: Private houses best serve their purposes when distinct and separate (modern Hippodamian plan), but parts of the city should retain older, maze-like constructions for safety in war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A city can and should have both sorts of buildings arranged so that elegance and safety are both consulted (e.g., plan some areas like rows of vines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Walls, bulwarks, and towers as functional ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Walls should include bulwarks and towers at proper places and distances; these defensive structures ought to be made ornamental as well as functional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Towers and bulwarks should combine defence with ornamentation; certain buildings for public tables and magistrates should be placed in towers/fortified spots as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of public buildings and squares
rubrics_metrics.description: Temples and the hall for public tables of chief magistrates should be contiguous and conspicuous; provide a large square for public tables into which mechanics/husbandmen should not enter without magistrate command, and a separate market square accessible by sea and land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place priests' public tables near temples; magistrates over contracts, indictments, and markets should be near the market square. Have a square for elders' gymnastic exercises and divide citizens into age-classes with officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of citizens' activities and age-based roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizens should be divided into distinct classes by age for exercises and duties: the young for what requires courage and obedience, the old for judgment and governance; education should reflect these differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Young should learn obedience (and courage), elders perform councils and gymnastic exercises with magistrates present to inspire modesty and fear; some aspects of education are the same, others different between governors and governed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ends of the state and legislator's purpose (happiness through virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best government is that in which citizens are happy; happiness consists in the energy and practice of virtue (not merely external goods), so the legislator must provide means and elements conducive to virtue and a worthy life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislator must know both the proper end and the means to it; supply things under fortune when possible but rely on knowledge and judgment to create a worthy state; aim education and laws at producing citizens who are good by nature, custom, and reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education aims and balance of nature, custom, and reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Education must form citizens by harmonising nature, custom, and reason; the soul is divided (reasoning and non-reasoning parts) and education should cultivate habits accordingly, prioritising bodily care first, then appetites, then reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since appetites and bodily aspects arise earlier than reason, care for body before soul; begin with proper customs that can correct or support reason; teach virtues that aim at rest (peace) rather than merely usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislator's priority: peace and safety over conquest
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislator should aim for rest and peace and the safety of those under governance, not the extension of despotism or conquest; prepare citizens to avoid being enslaved rather than to enslave others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training citizens only for war and conquest is mistaken—states preserved by war often ruin themselves in peace; laws should teach how to be at rest as well as how to defend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtues required for a happy polis
rubrics_metrics.description: A city ought to be temperate, brave, and patient; bravery and patience suit labour and war, philosophy suits rest, and temperance and justice are chief in time of peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different virtues are required in different conditions (war vs peace); in prosperity a higher degree of philosophy, temperance, and justice is necessary to prevent insolence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrustment of power by merit, courage, and age
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who have arms may insist on their own terms; the government must be entrusted to those possessing courage and judgment — courage more in the young, judgment more in the old — allocating parts according to different merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When different abilities are required (courage vs judgment) roles should be allotted accordingly; landed property and political power should be tied to those fit to exercise them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage timing and regulation for healthy offspring
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislator should regulate when citizens marry so bodily powers align: avoid fathers too young or too old and mothers too young or too old; recommended ages are roughly woman at eighteen, man at thirty-seven; observe season (winter) and proper spacing of children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marrying too early yields small, imperfect offspring and harms mothers; too large age gaps harm reverence and parental benefit; follow physicians and naturalists on particulars; proper bodily disposition will be considered in child education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical education and moderation of bodily regimen
rubrics_metrics.description: Children's bodily training should aim for a balanced constitution: neither the extreme habit of a wrestler nor infirmity; citizens should have a habit of labour but not excessively violent or narrowly specialised labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Body care precedes soul training; both men and women require moderate labour suitable for freemen, supporting later moral and civic excellence.
